content: Gluttony, derived from the Latin term gluttire, meaning to gulp down or to swallow, refers to the excessive indulgence and over-consumption of food, drink, or intoxicants to the point of wastefulness. In certain Christian traditions, gluttony is classified as one of the Seven Deadly Sins, representing a misplaced desire for food or the withholding of sustenance from those in need. Cultural perspectives on gluttony vary, with some societies viewing it as a vice, while others see it as a symbol of status. This perception is often influenced by the relative affluence of a society. For instance, wealthy groups may take pride in their ability to display an abundance of food, but this can provoke moral criticism when juxtaposed with the struggles of the less fortunate. Theologian Thomas Aquinas expanded the concept of gluttony, suggesting that it could also encompass an obsessive anticipation of meals, as well as the habitual consumption of delicacies and excessively expensive foods. Aquinas identified five specific ways in which gluttony could manifest: eating too soon (praepropere), eating food that is too costly (laute), eating in excessive quantities (nimis), eating with excessive eagerness (ardenter), and eating with excessive fastidiousness or daintiness (studiose). Pope Innocent XI condemned the notion that it is not sinful to eat or drink solely for the purpose of satisfying the palate. While it is not inherently wrong to derive pleasure from eating—since it is nearly impossible to consume food without experiencing some natural delight—it becomes a fault when eating is driven purely by sensual gratification, devoid of any rational purpose. Thus, even the most exquisite foods can be consumed without sin if the intent is virtuous and aligned with rationality, whereas consuming the simplest foods purely for pleasure can be considered a moral failing. In the Bible, gluttony is addressed through teachings on moderation (Ecclesiastes 7:18) and self-control (Galatians 5:23; Titus 2:12). Proverbs 23:2 warns against overindulgence, emphasizing the destructive physical consequences of excessive consumption of food or drink. Furthermore, gluttony can lead individuals to focus so intensely on physical desires that their spiritual lives are neglected or entirely forgotten. A historical example of this is Emperor Claudius of Rome, who, according to Suetonius, was infamous for his gluttony, indulging in extravagant feasts and even consuming priceless pearls dissolved in vinegar. In some social contexts, gluttony has been glorified, such as in competitive eating contests, which are often televised as public spectacles. A well-known example is Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest. In popular media, gluttony is frequently depicted as a character flaw or symbolic representation. For instance: In the television series Charmed, the character Piper Halliwell embodies gluttony in one episode. In Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Augustus Gloop represents gluttony through his insatiable appetite. In the film Se7en, the first murder victim is a representation of gluttony. In Garth Nix's The Keys to the Kingdom series, gluttony is personified by Drowned Wednesday, who takes the form of a massive Leviathan. In Fullmetal Alchemist, Gluttony is one of the seven homunculi, characterized by his ability to consume anything and his constant presence alongside Lust. In an Archie Comics newspaper strip from August 14, 2007, Jughead is humorously listed on Wikipedia under the term glutton.
